paragraphs: This paper addresses feature selection when the outcome is a function and the candidate predictors are ordinary scalar measurements. The challenge is to identify useful predictors from a very large collection while keeping computation manageable. The authors connect this functional regression problem to Group Elastic Net, developing an algorithm intended for settings with extremely many potential predictors.

The computational contribution is a solver that exploits sparsity in an Augmented Lagrangian formulation. Its efficiency comes from using that structure to reduce the work required during optimization. The authors then use properties of Functional Principal Components to extend the solver to function-on-scalar regression, bringing the computational improvement into a setting where responses have functional structure.

Simulations demonstrate CPU-time gains over the strongest existing competitors considered in the study. An application to a genome-wide association study of childhood obesity illustrates the method on real data. Together, these results support the approach as a computationally efficient way to perform feature selection for complex responses with many candidate explanatory variables.
neurips-2021-a-highly-efficient-group-el.tldr: A sparsity-aware Group Elastic Net solver speeds up feature selection and extends to regression with functional responses.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why small input changes can produce large output changes in ReLU networks whose parameters are independent Gaussian random variables. Its main result covers networks of constant depth across a broad range of layer widths. For example, it is sufficient for every layer's width to be polynomial in the width of any other layer.

The explanation comes from the networks' local behavior: near an input, their computed functions closely resemble random linear functions. This makes local sensitivity central to the existence of adversarial examples in the studied setting. The proof also identifies bottlenecks as important: the smallest layer encountered so far controls scales and sensitivities of the mapping through that portion of the network.

These findings extend earlier results for two-layer networks and networks whose widths decrease rapidly. The depth condition also has substantive meaning. The authors show that suitably deep networks can compute a nearly constant function with constant probability, so some restriction on depth is necessary for this kind of sensitivity result.
neurips-2021-adversarial-examples-in-mul.tldr: Constant-depth random Gaussian ReLU networks admit small input perturbations with large output effects because their local behavior resembles random linear functions.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether reinforcement learning becomes sample-efficient when the optimal action-value function can be expressed using a given collection of linear features. Earlier work showed that this representation assumption alone is insufficient. Here, the authors investigate a stronger condition: at every state, the best action has an optimal value separated from the second-best by a constant gap.

They prove that even this separation does not prevent an exponential sample-complexity lower bound in online reinforcement learning. A clearly better action can therefore remain difficult to discover through interaction, despite the existence of a compact linear representation. The result rules out constant action separation as a sufficient remedy for the online learning difficulty.

The conclusion differs for access to a generative model, where sample-efficient learning is possible under the constant-gap condition. This establishes an exponential separation between the two access settings. The paper also provides positive results: additional low-variance or hypercontractivity assumptions each enable provably sample-efficient reinforcement learning.
neurips-2021-an-exponential-lower-bound-.tldr: Linear realizability and a constant action-value gap still permit exponential sample requirements in online reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Causal identification asks whether a causal effect can be computed from available distributions together with assumptions about how a system works. Many algorithms answer this through graphical rules. Other results show that proxy variables can recover certain otherwise inaccessible effects by solving matrix equations. This paper develops an algorithm that combines these two approaches.

The authors first characterize connections between particular formulas derived from causal graphs and matrix multiplication. Those connections let them expand the conditions under which proxy variables support identification. They also introduce intermediate criteria based on a matrix pseudoinverse, adding algebraic tools to the reasoning process used to establish whether an effect is recoverable.

The resulting algorithm accepts a collection of marginal, conditional, and interventional distributions and integrates the enriched matrix criteria into graphical identification. Its contribution is a broader route from causal assumptions and available evidence to identifiable effects. Recovery remains tied to the relevant identification conditions; the advance is in the range of conditions the algorithm can use.
neurips-2021-causal-identification-with-.tldr: A causal identification algorithm combines graphical reasoning with matrix equations to broaden the use of proxy variables.

paragraphs: The paper studies semi-supervised object detection, where unlabeled images supplement a smaller labeled collection. This setting is attractive because collecting detection labels is labor-intensive. However, pseudo labels can introduce noisy regions that mislead training. The authors focus on understanding and reducing that regional noise so unlabeled data can contribute more effectively.

They first examine the adverse effects of different forms of pseudo-label noise. Their proposed method then quantifies uncertainty at the region level by identifying noise-resistant properties across different strengths. This places the reliability of individual regions inside the learning procedure, making uncertainty part of how the detector learns from its generated labels.

The training approach combines region uncertainty quantification with encouragement of probability outputs that can have multiple peaks. The authors present this combination as a way to achieve learning that resists noisy labeling. Experiments on PASCAL VOC and MS COCO report strong performance, supporting the usefulness of region-level uncertainty for semi-supervised detection in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2021-combating-noise-semi-superv.tldr: Region-level uncertainty helps semi-supervised object detectors resist noisy pseudo labels during training.

paragraphs: GANformer2 generates scenes through an iterative process organized around objects. Its design explicitly reflects the idea that a visual scene contains components with relationships to one another. By building this structure into the model, the authors aim to make image generation more efficient, controllable, and interpretable.

Generation has two stages. A lightweight planning stage drafts a high-level scene layout, and an attention-based execution stage refines that layout into a detailed image. The sequence progresses from a rough sketch toward a layout accounting for object depths and dependencies, then to the final depiction. This gives the generation process intermediate structure that can be examined.

Evaluations range from multi-object CLEVR scenes to COCO images. The authors report state-of-the-art results for visual quality, diversity, and consistency across their evaluation. Additional experiments examine disentanglement and reveal how the scene develops step by step. The findings support an explicitly compositional architecture as an effective approach to generating both structured scenes and complex real-world imagery.
neurips-2021-compositional-transformers-.tldr: GANformer2 generates images by planning object-based scene layouts and progressively refining them with attention.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the loss of image quality that GANs experience when training data are scarce. Existing approaches often use augmentation while keeping the discriminator's task focused on separating real images from generated ones. InsGen expands that task so the discriminator must also distinguish individual images, whether they come from the dataset or the generator.

This instance-level objective allows the discriminator to learn from an unlimited stream of synthesized samples, helping alleviate overfitting to a small real dataset. The method also introduces noise perturbations to strengthen discrimination. The generator, in turn, uses the learned ability to distinguish instances as a signal encouraging diverse outputs.

Experiments across multiple datasets and training settings support the method's effectiveness. With 2,000 FFHQ training images, the authors report a 23.5% FID improvement over the state-of-the-art approach used for comparison. The result illustrates how changing what the discriminator learns can improve data efficiency while also encouraging diversity in the images produced.
neurips-2021-data-efficient-instance-gen.tldr: InsGen improves GAN training with limited data by teaching the discriminator to distinguish individual real and generated images.

paragraphs: The paper develops a mathematical connection between neural networks and Gaussian process models, motivated by their complementary strengths and weaknesses. Its central result establishes an equivalence between neural-network forward passes and forward passes in sparse Gaussian process models, including deep versions. This connects the computations used to make predictions in the two model families.

The theory interprets neural-network activation functions as interdomain inducing features. The authors obtain this interpretation by analyzing how activation functions interact with kernels. That relationship supplies the mathematical basis for constructing models that admit both a neural-network interpretation and a sparse Gaussian process interpretation, linking architectural choices to probabilistic modeling.

The resulting models can be viewed as neural networks with better uncertainty prediction or as deep Gaussian processes with better predictive accuracy. Experiments on regression and classification datasets support those improvements. The contribution therefore combines a theoretical correspondence with models intended to bring useful properties of each approach into the other, with empirical support on the studied prediction tasks.
neurips-2021-deep-neural-networks-as-poi.tldr: A forward-pass equivalence connects neural networks to sparse deep Gaussian processes and supports models with improved uncertainty or accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to choose parameters of congestion games so that selfish behavior leads to desirable equilibria. Such problems arise in the design of traffic and communication networks. They are difficult because the designer's optimization depends on players' equilibrium behavior, while the players themselves may choose among enormous collections of combinatorial strategies.

The proposed method combines differentiable optimization with zero-suppressed binary decision diagrams, which can represent strategy sets compactly. It numerically approximates an equilibrium and uses automatic differentiation to measure how that approximation changes with game parameters. These derivatives allow gradient-based optimization of the designer's choices within the Stackelberg formulation.

The algorithm is designed to incorporate Nesterov acceleration and exploit the compactness that decision diagrams exhibit empirically. Together, these properties let it handle games with vast strategy collections without treating every strategy as an isolated item. Experiments on real network-design instances demonstrate practical applicability, supporting the combination of compact representations and differentiable equilibrium computation.
neurips-2021-differentiable-equilibrium-.tldr: Compact decision diagrams and differentiable equilibrium approximations enable gradient-based design of large combinatorial congestion games.

paragraphs: This paper develops differentially private stochastic optimization algorithms for several convex and non-convex settings. For convex problems, it focuses on non-smooth generalized linear losses. Exploiting this particular family allows stronger efficiency and accuracy results than those available for general non-smooth convex losses.

In the Euclidean setting, the convex algorithm achieves optimal excess population risk in near-linear time. In the l1 setting, it achieves nearly optimal risk with logarithmic dependence on dimension, avoiding a dimension-dependent lower bound that applies to the broader loss family. For non-convex problems, the goal is instead to approximate stationary points. The authors give linear-time algorithms for smooth constrained problems, including a nearly dimension-independent rate under l1 geometry and polyhedral constraints.

They also introduce a method for non-smooth weakly convex optimization in Euclidean geometry. Its rate matches the best existing non-private algorithm when dimension is at most on the order of the square root of sample size. The non-convex Euclidean results extend to lp geometries for 1 < p ≤ 2 with only polylogarithmic dimension overhead.
neurips-2021-differentially-private-stoc.tldr: New private optimization algorithms improve computational and statistical guarantees under specified loss, constraint, and geometry assumptions.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes stochastic gradient methods with momentum on a high-dimensional random least-squares problem. Using a framework inspired by random matrix theory, it gives an exact deterministic characterization of their sequence of objective values in terms of the Hessian's eigenvalues. This connects optimization behavior to the curvature structure of the studied problem.

The characterization yields simple expressions for nearly optimal hyperparameters, average-case complexity, and the limiting neighborhood reached by the algorithms. One consequence is that small-batch stochastic heavy-ball momentum with a fixed momentum parameter offers no actual improvement over SGD when step sizes are adjusted appropriately. In the non-strongly convex setting, however, momentum can produce a large improvement.

The authors introduce sDANA, a stochastic Nesterov-style method whose hyperparameters depend on the number of samples. It achieves asymptotically optimal average-case complexity while retaining linear convergence in the strongly convex setting without parameter adjustment. These results clarify when momentum helps within the analyzed quadratic model and motivate parameters that adapt to sample count.
neurips-2021-dynamics-of-stochastic-mome.tldr: An exact analysis of random quadratic problems clarifies momentum's benefits and motivates the sample-dependent sDANA algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper assesses how robust a trained neural network is to uncertainty in its inputs. It formulates this assessment as a statistical hypothesis test: local robustness depends on whether the estimated probability of failure falls below a chosen critical level. This turns robustness assessment into a question about failure frequency under the input uncertainties being considered.

The procedure uses Importance Splitting, a stochastic simulation method for generating samples of rare events. Its role is to make failures accessible to estimation even when they occur infrequently. The approach draws on statistical reliability engineering, connecting neural-network evaluation to methods designed to assess systems whose failures may be rare.

The authors derive theoretical guarantees that apply at finite sample sizes, rather than only in a large-sample limit. Experiments involving large networks indicate that the assessment can be efficient while requiring relatively few network evaluations. The resulting robustness judgment is specifically statistical and local: it concerns a failure-probability threshold under the assessed uncertainties.
neurips-2021-efficient-statistical-asses.tldr: Rare-event simulation enables efficient statistical tests of local neural-network robustness with finite-sample guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to compare classification performance with the best accuracy theoretically possible for a data distribution. That reference is determined by Bayes error, which is usually difficult to compute. The authors show how to compute it exactly for generative distributions learned with normalizing flows, creating benchmarks with a known optimal error.

The key mathematical fact is that invertible transformations preserve Bayes error. This lets the authors work with the flow models' Gaussian base distributions and use Holmes-Diaconis-Ross integration for efficient computation. Changing the models' temperature also produces synthetic datasets resembling standard benchmarks while allowing almost any desired Bayes error.

These controlled datasets let the authors investigate how close leading classifiers come to the theoretical optimum. They find near-optimal accuracy in some cases, but not all, and use the method to assess the intrinsic difficulty of standard benchmarks. The exact error calculation applies to the learned generative models, providing a concrete reference for evaluating classifiers on those modeled distributions.
neurips-2021-evaluating-state-of-the-art.tldr: Normalizing-flow models enable synthetic classification benchmarks with known Bayes error, revealing when classifiers approach optimal accuracy.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering organizes data through repeated divisions into progressively smaller groups. This paper studies that task using Dasgupta's cost function and develops two polynomial-time approximation algorithms. Their constant-factor guarantees mean the resulting hierarchy's cost stays within a fixed multiplicative factor of the optimum for the graph families covered by the results.

The first algorithm applies to high-conductance graphs. Its simple construction avoids the complicated recursive searches for sparse cuts used in earlier work. The main algorithm covers a broad family of graphs with clearly defined cluster structure, extending guarantees that previously applied only to graphs generated by stochastic models.

The contribution therefore broadens the structural conditions under which efficient hierarchical clustering has a strong approximation guarantee. The authors also evaluate their approach on synthetic and real datasets. In those experiments, the proposed algorithm outperforms the earlier algorithm intended for graphs with well-defined clusters, adding empirical support to the theoretical extension beyond stochastic graph-generation assumptions.
neurips-2021-hierarchical-clustering-o-1.tldr: Two efficient hierarchical clustering algorithms achieve constant-factor guarantees for high-conductance and broadly defined well-clustered graphs.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how a Transformer can use source code's syntax-tree structure when learning code representations. Its starting point is that code modeling requires attention to syntax and semantics, and that paths through syntax trees provide useful structural information. The authors study two established forms of path encoding and integrate them into Transformer attention.

One encoding describes the tree path connecting a pair of code tokens. The other describes the path from each token's leaf node to the tree root. Inspired by positional encoding, the method incorporates both kinds of information into a unified architecture. This allows the study to examine how relationships between tokens interact with each token's position in the syntax tree.

The empirical investigation leads to TPTrans, a representation model that outperforms strong baselines in the reported evaluation. Experiments and ablation studies on code summarization across four languages support the approach. The findings indicate that explicitly incorporating tree paths into attention can improve the code representations used for summarization.
neurips-2021-integrating-tree-path-in-tr.tldr: TPTrans integrates token-to-token and token-to-root syntax-tree paths into Transformer attention to improve code summarization.

paragraphs: Optimal feedback control models can explain many aspects of human sensorimotor behavior when they include signal-dependent noise. Such analyses commonly assume a task's cost function and compare predicted movements with observed ones. This paper develops an inverse approach that infers the cost function from behavior while accounting for that noise structure.

The authors formulate the task as a partially observable Markov decision process and distinguish the acting person's inference problem from the experimenter's. They derive a probabilistic description of how states and belief states evolve, together with an approximate propagation equation for the linear-quadratic Gaussian case with signal-dependent noise. They also allow the experimenter to observe only part of the state.

Validation on synthetic data and application to experimental data demonstrate the approach's feasibility. The framework provides a way to recover costs and benefits implicit in sequential sensorimotor behavior. It thereby connects explanations based on optimal action selection with descriptions grounded in observed behavior, while explicitly accounting for uncertainty faced by both actor and observer.
neurips-2021-inverse-optimal-control-ada.tldr: An inverse-control framework infers human sensorimotor costs while accounting for signal-dependent noise and partial observation.

paragraphs: Retrosynthesis prediction starts with a target molecule and seeks precursor molecules that could be used to make it. This paper designs a graph-based model around a chemical observation: much of the precursor graph's topology remains unchanged during a reaction. That motivates predicting localized structural changes while retaining the larger molecular organization.

The model works in two stages. First, it predicts graph edits that turn the target into incomplete molecular structures called synthons. It then completes those structures by attaching appropriate leaving groups. This division makes the prediction process easier to interpret because it exposes both the proposed structural changes and the subsequent completion of the precursors.

The authors report that this decomposition simplifies the architecture and makes predictions amenable to manual correction. Their model achieves 53.7% top-1 accuracy, exceeding previous template-free and semi-template-based approaches in the reported comparison. The result supports aligning a model's intermediate steps with chemical reasoning as a useful design choice for retrosynthesis prediction.
neurips-2021-learning-graph-models-for-r.tldr: A two-stage graph model predicts retrosynthetic edits and completes precursor molecules, improving interpretability and reported prediction accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper asks which aspect of convolution matters more for learning: processing local portions of an input or treating translated patterns equivalently. It investigates this through teacher-student kernel regression, using convolutional kernels inspired by simple neural tangent kernels. The teacher and student have specified filter sizes, allowing the analysis to distinguish locality from translation invariance.

Using heuristic methods from physics, the authors find that locality determines the learning-curve exponent in the ridgeless setting, whereas translation invariance does not. This exponent describes how test error decreases as the training set grows. When the teacher's filter is smaller than the student's, the exponent depends only on the student's filter size and not on overall input dimension.

Experiments confirm the predicted exponents. The paper also proves, under a universality assumption, that a ridge penalty decreasing with training-set size gives similar exponents. These findings identify a mechanism by which local structure can avoid dimension-dependent learning rates in the studied kernel-regression scenarios.
neurips-2021-locality-defeats-the-curse-.tldr: In studied convolutional kernel models, locality can make learning-curve exponents independent of input dimension under specified filter-size conditions.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning uses a learned account of environment dynamics to improve policy learning from experience. Latent dynamics models make this possible in a compact representation of high-dimensional observations. This paper argues that imagination can be restricted when it considers only memories derived from actual experiences, and proposes Imagining with Derived Memory, or IDM.

Inspired by the idea of a memory prosthesis, IDM enriches the diversity of imagined experience available for policy learning. It also weights that imagination by prediction reliability. The combination aims to provide more varied learning material while accounting for how dependable the model's predictions are, linking the amount of imagined experience to its usefulness.

Experiments examine high-dimensional visual control tasks in the DMControl benchmark. The authors report stronger policy robustness than previous state-of-the-art methods and improved sample efficiency for model-based learning. These findings support enriching the imagination process as a way to make better use of learned dynamics in the evaluated control tasks.
neurips-2021-model-based-reinforcement-l.tldr: IDM enriches imagined experience and weights it by prediction reliability to improve visual-control policy robustness and sample efficiency.

paragraphs: The paper studies whether observed rankings are uniformly distributed when the alternative is restricted to single-parameter Mallows models. A ranking over many items belongs to a factorially large set of possible orderings, making direct treatment of the full domain challenging. The method instead exploits structure in the alternative distribution through simple pairwise statistics.

The authors show that these statistics can distinguish uniform rankings from the specified alternatives with a sample requirement scaling as the inverse square root of the number of items. Their result permits testing with only two samples when there are sufficiently many items. This unusually favorable scaling relies on the restricted testing problem considered.

The paper also develops a central differentially private algorithm whose sample requirement depends on the privacy budget and item count. Because the method uses binary statistics extracted from rankings, it transfers straightforwardly to the local privacy setting. Large-scale experiments, including rankings over 10,000 items, demonstrate favorable scaling as the number of items grows.
neurips-2021-private-and-non-private-uni.tldr: Pairwise ranking statistics enable sample-efficient uniformity tests against single-parameter Mallows alternatives, including private variants.

paragraphs: Quantization reduces a neural network's memory and inference costs by representing parameters at lower precision. It also changes those parameters and can alter predictions. This paper investigates whether an adversary can deliberately shape that behavioral difference so malicious behavior becomes active when the model is quantized.

The authors adapt quantization-aware training into a framework for creating such outcomes. They demonstrate three forms: broad accuracy degradation, attacks on particular samples, and a backdoor controlled by an input trigger. A single compromised model can affect multiple quantization schemes in their study, including techniques intended to make quantization robust.

The paper also demonstrates a federated-learning scenario in which collaborating malicious participants inject a quantization-activated backdoor. Its countermeasure investigation finds that only retraining consistently removes the attack artifacts among the approaches considered. The findings identify quantization as a transformation whose security implications can extend beyond ordinary accuracy changes, because training can deliberately embed behavior that appears after precision reduction.
neurips-2021-qu-anti-zation-exploiting-q.tldr: Adversarial training can embed harmful model behavior that activates after quantization, including targeted errors and backdoors.

paragraphs: Transductive few-shot methods use the unlabeled query set's collective statistics to improve predictions from a small labeled set. The paper questions evaluations that make every query set perfectly class-balanced. That arrangement fixes class proportions to a uniform distribution, whereas practical query sets can have unknown and unequal proportions.

The authors construct evaluation tasks with class probabilities sampled from a Dirichlet distribution, allowing varying class mixtures within existing benchmarks. Across three widely used datasets, leading transductive methods experience substantial performance drops. Some even fall below inductive methods, showing that their apparent advantage can depend strongly on the balance built into the evaluation.

The paper also proposes an alpha-divergence generalization of the mutual-information loss to handle changing class distributions. Its optimization method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across the evaluated datasets, models, and few-shot settings. The contribution combines a more varied testing protocol with an objective designed for that variation, making class proportions an explicit part of assessing few-shot performance.
neurips-2021-realistic-evaluation-of-tra.tldr: Unequal query-class proportions expose weaknesses in transductive few-shot methods, while an alpha-divergence objective improves performance under this variation.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the reliability of local explanations for black-box predictions. Existing explanation techniques can produce unstable feature importances while offering little indication of how uncertain those estimates are. The authors develop a Bayesian framework that generates explanations together with uncertainty, giving users more information about the reliability of the reported feature contributions.

They instantiate the framework as Bayesian versions of LIME and KernelSHAP. These methods return credible intervals around feature importances, expressing uncertainty as a range with an associated posterior probability. The authors also report improved consistency and stability, connecting uncertainty modeling to the repeatability of the resulting explanations.

A theoretical analysis uses the uncertainty estimates to determine how many perturbations to sample and how to sample for faster convergence. This makes uncertainty useful both for interpreting an explanation and for controlling its computational cost. Experiments on multiple real datasets and user studies support the framework's effectiveness, alongside the paper's guarantees for efficient, reliable local explanation.
neurips-2021-reliable-post-hoc-explanati.tldr: Bayesian versions of LIME and KernelSHAP quantify feature-importance uncertainty and use it to improve explanation stability and sampling efficiency.

paragraphs: TacticZero applies deep reinforcement learning to interactive theorem proving. It learns proof-search strategies together with predictions of tactics and their arguments in an end-to-end framework. This brings decisions about how to proceed through a proof into the same learning process as decisions about which proof operations to attempt.

The authors represent theorem proving as a Markov decision process whose states contain sets of potential derivation paths. This representation supports a backtracking mechanism: the agent can discard a path it predicts will lead nowhere and resume from a promising alternative. The search process therefore includes learned decisions about abandoning and revisiting possible routes to a proof.

The framework is implemented in the HOL theorem prover. On unseen problems, the learned search strategies outperform the existing automated provers, or hammers, available in HOL in the reported evaluation. Ablation studies investigate the roles of key components. The results support jointly learning proof operations and search management within the tested theorem-proving environment.
neurips-2021-tacticzero-learning-to-prov.tldr: TacticZero learns tactics, arguments, and backtracking strategies together, improving automated proof search on unseen HOL problems.

paragraphs: The paper revisits spatial attention in vision Transformers, focusing on a design choice the authors identify as central to dense prediction performance. It shows that a carefully designed, simple attention mechanism can compare favorably with state-of-the-art schemes. This investigation leads to two architectures, Twins-PCPVT and Twins-SVT.

The proposed architectures emphasize both computational efficiency and ease of implementation. Their operations involve matrix multiplications that modern deep-learning frameworks already optimize heavily. That connection matters because the design's computational ingredients fit established execution machinery, making simplicity part of the practical case for the architectures alongside their prediction performance.

The authors report strong results across image classification, object detection, and segmentation. These tasks span whole-image decisions and spatially detailed predictions, giving the evaluation a broad visual scope. The combination of simplicity, efficiency, and reported performance suggests that the architectures may serve as stronger backbones for multiple vision tasks, with the findings supporting that possibility across the evaluated applications.
neurips-2021-twins-revisiting-the-design.tldr: Twins-PCPVT and Twins-SVT use simple, efficient spatial attention and achieve strong results across classification, detection, and segmentation.
